analysis.one_liner: Bans price-gouging on gasoline and heating fuels during declared energy emergencies.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 217-207 on May 19, 2022, with every voting Republican opposed; the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During a declared energy emergency, the bill would make it illegal to sell gasoline, diesel, heating oil, jet fuel, or other consumer fuels at prices that are unconscionably excessive and that exploit the emergency. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the ban, and fines collected would fund home energy assistance for low-income households. The bill would also double the fine for oil-market manipulation, extend anti-manipulation rules to more fuels, direct the FTC to investigate whether refinery closures are being used to manipulate gasoline prices, and create an FTC unit to monitor fuel markets. The House passed it on May 19, 2022, 217-207, but the Senate placed it on its calendar without ever holding a vote, and it expired at the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and households that buy heating oil or propane, especially low-income households, who would get protection from emergency-driven price spikes and whose home energy assistance fund would receive fines collected from violators.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans selling consumer fuels at unconscionably excessive prices during a President-proclaimed energy emergency, covering gasoline, diesel, heating oil, jet fuel, propane, natural gas, and biofuels at both wholesale and retail.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban, giving priority to companies with more than $500 million a year in consumer-fuel sales, and state attorneys general could sue retail sellers for penalties and restitution for state residents.
Civil penalties collected by the FTC would go into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund used for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the Weatherization Assistance Program.

The FTC would have to investigate whether gasoline prices are being manipulated by reducing refinery capacity or other practices, and would establish a Transportation Fuel Monitoring and Enforcement Unit to continuously collect and analyze crude oil and fuel market data.
The bill extends existing prohibitions on market manipulation and false price reporting to all transportation fuels and doubles the penalty for violations from $1 million to $2 million.
The Energy Information Administration would survey energy companies and publish detailed price and volume data to make crude oil and transportation fuel markets more transparent and competitive.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and wholesale and retail fuel sellers, who would face fines, lawsuits by state attorneys general, mandatory data surveys, and a ban on raising prices beyond increased costs during emergencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and fuel sellers

drawbacks.text: The ban only takes effect when the President declares an energy emergency, so protection depends on presidential discretion to invoke it for specific fuels and areas; the proclamation lasts up to 30 days at a time but can be renewed.

Price-gouging bans can be hard to apply in volatile fuel markets, since sellers legitimately face fast-changing wholesale costs; the bill tries to handle this with an affirmative defense for price increases that reasonably reflect additional costs or risks, and it excludes futures-market transactions.

The bill creates new reporting and enforcement duties for the FTC and the Energy Information Administration, with appropriations left to future Congresses, so its monitoring unit and surveys depend on funding that was never enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing fuel-driven price spikes, the protection and the LIHEAP funding are concrete, and the bill tries to avoid punishing legitimate cost increases through the cost-based affirmative defense. The main limits are practical: the ban operates only during declared emergencies, and anti-gouging cases require proving prices were unconscionably excessive rather than driven by real supply costs. The market-transparency and manipulation provisions are the longer-term value, but they too depend on appropriations that never followed because the bill never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 217-207, but after the Senate received it and put it on its calendar in May 2022, no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 6, 2022, by Rep. Kim Schrier with 16 Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor Committees.
On May 19, 2022, a Republican motion to recommit the bill to committee failed 201-220, with all 201 voting Republicans in favor and 219 of 220 voting Democrats opposed.
The House passed the bill later that day, 217-207: 217 of 221 voting Democrats in favor, all 4 voting Democrats opposed being Democrats, and 0 of 208 Republicans voting yes with 203 voting no.
The Senate received the bill the same day, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 373), but no floor vote ever occurred.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the Senate acting on the bill.

The passed-House version added the FTC investigation of gasoline price manipulation, the Transportation Fuel Monitoring and Enforcement Unit, the extension of anti-manipulation rules to all transportation fuels, and the Energy Information Administration market-surveys provisions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil and gas companies and fuel sellers are better off: no federal emergency price-gouging ban, no doubled manipulation penalties, no FTC fuel-market monitoring unit, and no mandatory market data surveys ever took effect.

for.name: 217 of 221 House Democrats
for.role: House Democratic voting bloc on final passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 217-4, supplying every yes vote.

against.name: 203 of 208 House Republicans
against.role: House Republican voting bloc on final passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 203-0 among those voting, defeating the bill's chances in a closely divided Congress.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in May 2022.

against.name: Rep. Bruce Westerman
against.role: House Republican, mover of the motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to the Energy and Commerce Committee, a motion that failed 201-220.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 217 of 221 voting Democrats voted yes and every one of the 203 voting Republicans voted no; the motion to recommit split the same way, 201 Republicans for and 219 Democrats against.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would subject them to emergency price-gouging penalties, a doubled $2 million manipulation penalty extended to more fuels, an FTC investigation into refinery-capacity reductions, and mandatory Energy Information Administration market surveys. Their pricing during supply emergencies is exactly what the bill targets, so their interest ran against the consumers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Wholesale and retail fuel sellers (gas stations, heating-oil dealers)
industries.note: State attorneys general could sue retail sellers for penalties and restitution, and the FTC would prioritize enforcement against sellers with over $500 million in annual consumer-fuel sales. Sellers gain an affirmative defense if price increases reasonably reflect their own higher costs, so honest cost pass-through is protected while emergency profiteering is penalized.

The bill includes ethanol, biomass-based diesel, and renewable blending components in the definitions of consumer fuel and transportation fuel, putting them under the same anti-gouging and anti-manipulation rules as petroleum fuels for the first time.

industries.industry: Low-income energy assistance programs (LIHEAP and weatherization)
industries.note: All FTC-collected penalties would go into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the Weatherization Assistance Program, giving low-income households direct relief funded by gouging fines.
